title: Read: tones and first characters
description: Tones first, then your first hanzi.

units.title: The four tones
intro: Mandarin is written with characters called hanzi. Each character is one syllable and has a meaning.
Pinyin spells the sound of a character with Latin letters, like 'ma'. It is a helper, the same way romaji helps with Japanese.
The mark above the vowel is the tone: how your voice moves while you say the syllable. A different tone makes a different word.
1st tone (mā): high and flat, like holding one sung note. 2nd tone (má): rising, like asking 'what?'
3rd tone (mǎ): low and dipping, like a doubtful 'well...'. 4th tone (mà): a sharp fall, like a firm 'No!'
Neutral tone (ma): no mark. Short and light.
In this unit the same syllable, 'ma', is five different words. Listen to each one a few times before you move on.

items.hint: 1st tone: high and flat. The flat line over the a is the shape of your voice.
2nd tone: rising. The mark climbs upward, and so does your voice.

items.meaning: horse (3rd tone: dips low, then rises)
items.hint: 3rd tone: dips low. The mark is a small valley: go down, then a little up.
4th tone: sharp fall. The mark drops, like a scolding 'No!'
Neutral tone: light and short. Put 吗 at the end of a sentence to make it a yes/no question.

units.title: Numbers 1 to 5
intro: Numbers are a good first set of hanzi. The first three are just lines you can count.
Reading pinyin: 'yī' sounds like 'ee'. 'èr' sounds like 'are'. 'sān' sounds like 'sahn'.
'sì' is the tricky one: the i after s is not 'ee'. Say 's' and keep buzzing, like 'sz'. 'wǔ' sounds like 'woo'.
Watch the tone marks. They tell you how to move your voice, just like in the last unit.

items.hint: One line means one. 1st tone: high and flat, like the line itself.
Two lines mean two. 4th tone: falling.
Three lines mean three. 1st tone: high and flat.
A box with four sides, like a window with curtains. 4th tone: falling.
A shape standing between a top line and a bottom line. 3rd tone: dipping.

units.title: Numbers 6 to 10
intro: Five more and you can count to ten.
Reading pinyin: 'q' sounds like 'ch', so 'qī' is 'chee'. 'j' is a soft 'j', so 'jiǔ' is close to 'jyoh'.
'shí' is not 'she'. The i after sh sounds like 'r': say 'shr' with a rising voice. 'liù' is close to 'lyoh', 'bā' is 'bah'.
Then the fun part. Bigger numbers are built from pieces: 十一 is ten-one, which is 11. 二十 is two-ten, which is 20.

items.hint: A person with a hat, arms out and legs apart. 4th tone: falling.
Like an upside-down 7 with a line through it. 1st tone: high and flat.
Two strokes leaning apart. 1st tone: high and flat.
Close to a cross, but with a hooked tail: nine is almost ten. 3rd tone: dipping.
A cross, like a plus sign. 2nd tone: rising.

units.title: You and me
intro: Many hanzi are built from smaller parts, and the parts give clues. Watch the left side of the characters in this unit.
亻 on the left is a squeezed form of 人, person. 女 on the left means woman.
Reading pinyin: 'wǒ' is close to 'waw'. 'nǐ' is 'nee'. 'tā' is 'tah'. 'hǎo' is 'how'.
他 (he) and 她 (she) sound exactly the same. You can only tell them apart in writing.

items.hint: I, me. Many strokes, but you will see it so often it sticks. 3rd tone: dipping.
亻 (person) on the left: the person in front of me is you. 3rd tone: dipping.
亻 (person) on the left: he. 1st tone: high and flat.
女 (woman) on the left: she. Same sound as 他.
女 (woman) next to 子 (child): together they mean good. 3rd tone: dipping.

units.title: Small words
intro: Five characters that show up in almost every sentence.
Reading pinyin: 'rén' starts with a buzzing r, tongue curled back. 'dà' is 'dah'. 'xiǎo' is close to 'shyow': x is a soft sh.
是 is 'to be'. Mandarin uses the same word for am, is and are. No changes to memorize.
不 means 'not'. It is 'bù', but in front of another falling tone it flips to rising: 不是 is 'bú shì'.

items.hint: A person walking, seen from the side: two legs. 2nd tone: rising.
A person stretching both arms out wide: big. 4th tone: falling.
A center stroke with two small strokes falling away from it: small. 3rd tone: dipping.
To be. 日 (sun) sits on top. 'shr' with a sharp fall.
Not. A line on top, like a lid holding things down. 4th tone: falling.

units.title: Sun, moon, fire, water
intro: Some of the oldest hanzi started as drawings. These five still look a little like what they mean.
Reading pinyin: 'shuǐ' is close to 'shway'. 'huǒ' is 'hwaw'. 'shān' is 'shahn'. 'yuè' is 'yweh'.
'rì' is hard: curl your tongue back and buzz, like the r in 'run' held on its own, with a falling voice.
日 also means day, and 月 also means month. So 一月 is month one: January.

items.hint: A stream down the middle with splashes on both sides. 3rd tone: dipping.
A fire with a spark flying off each side. 3rd tone: dipping.
Three peaks: a mountain. 1st tone: high and flat.
It began as a circle with a dot: the sun. Also means day. 4th tone: falling.
A crescent moon standing upright. Also means month. 4th tone: falling.

units.title: Have, eat, drink
intro: Three everyday verbs and the name of the country.
口 is a mouth. Both 吃 (eat) and 喝 (drink) have it on the left.
Reading pinyin: 'yǒu' sounds like 'yo'. 'zhōng' is close to 'jong'. 'guó' is 'gwaw'. 'chī' is 'chr', high and flat. 'hē' is close to 'huh'.
中国 is 'middle country': China. Add 人 and you get 中国人, a Chinese person.

items.hint: To have. The bottom looks like 月. Picture a hand on top holding it. 3rd tone: dipping.
A line straight through the middle of a box: middle. 1st tone: high and flat.
A border around something precious: country. 2nd tone: rising.
口 (mouth) on the left: eat. 1st tone: high and flat.
口 (mouth) on the left again: drink. 1st tone: high and flat.
